newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait bourse dips, Central Bank urges caution.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait bourse dips, Central Bank urges caution.

text.p: The Kuwait Stock Exchange index opened one percent lower on Wednesday after the central bank governor voiced discomfort with increased speculation by groups of big investors and gyrating share prices.

Shedding slightly more than Tuesday's gain, the index at 0900 GMT was 30 points down at 2,299.5. Wednesday is the last trading day of the week which has been marked by conflicting statements with MPs warning of a market crash while the government said the situation was "reassuring".

"The Governor warned of some practices by an effective party of big investors and the forming of undeclared alliances and unwritten accords with the aim of affecting developments...," the Kuwait News Agency quoted bank governor Sheikh Salem Abdul-Aziz al-Sabah as saying late on Tuesday.
Analysts, commenting on fears of a crash, told Reuters on Tuesday that some big investors were forming trading pools to drive prices up, and warned of negative effects on small investors.
Sheikh Salem voiced discomfort with what he described as economically unjustified rises and occasional sharp swings in prices of some shares that are not driven by fundamentals.

He attributed the recent records to the increase in capital flows to the market from private sector deposits with banks, credit extended by banks for securities trade purposes and capital flows from abroad.
Some analysts say the market could witness a correction and warned that borrowing for equity trading was at a high level, but they did not give a figure.

Fears of a correction emerged late last year as trading value soared above $160 million a day but talk of a crash gained steam when the daily value hit $414 million and the index set a record of 2,354.7 on April 27.
The word crash revives memories of the 1982 collapse of Kuwait's unregulated Manakh bourse, resulting in a debt of over $20 billion which the government is still trying to resolve.

"I do not advocate (state) interference in the market but instead of down playing, the government should warn of a danger in exaggerated trading and also make it very clear that it would not step in again to help the people," leading Kuwaiti economist Jassem al-Saadoun told Reuters on Tuesday night.
